ruled_out.assertion: f-string interpolation of account_id into a text() SQL statement is SQL injection
ruled_out.killed_by: The route is declared @api_bp.get('/accounts/<int:account_id>/balance') at api.py:56; Flask's int converter matches only digits and passes a Python int, so no attacker-controlled string reaches the query.

ruled_out.assertion: _compare_legacy_digest performs a non-constant-time secret comparison
ruled_out.killed_by: grep over the whole tree returns only the definition; no caller exists, and the docstring records that the migration removed the last one.

ruled_out.assertion: import_batch resolves a caller-supplied filename under the import root and is traversable
ruled_out.killed_by: _staged_path canonicalises with os.path.realpath and rejects anything not under os.path.realpath(root)+os.sep at importer.py:28 before the file is opened.

ruled_out.assertion: subprocess.run in _transcode is command injection
ruled_out.killed_by: The command is an argument list with no shell, and the only variable, source, comes from the ENCODINGS dict lookup at importer.py:37-39, which raises for anything else.

ruled_out.assertion: State-changing API endpoints authorised by a session cookie have no CSRF token
ruled_out.killed_by: config.py:25 sets SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE='Lax', which suppresses the cookie on cross-site POST and DELETE; the state-changing routes are all unsafe methods, which is the exculpation WEB-15 names.

ruled_out.assertion: LIMIT is interpolated into the notifications query
ruled_out.killed_by: The only caller is routes/notifications.js:32, whose Fastify schema declares limit as an integer with minimum 1 and maximum 200 (notifications.js:10); ajv coerces and validates before the handler runs.

ruled_out.assertion: execRaw executes arbitrary SQL
ruled_out.killed_by: No HTTP route or module in the tree calls it; grep returns the definition and the export only.

ruled_out.assertion: config.defaults.demoToken is a leaked credential
ruled_out.killed_by: The value is the literal 'pulse-sample-token-for-docs' and no code reads config.defaults except the /admin/config response; it is a documented sample, not a live credential. The disclosure of the whole config object is covered by the unauthenticated-admin finding.

ruled_out.assertion: quote() is an unsafe hand-rolled SQL escaper
ruled_out.killed_by: It doubles single quotes, which is correct for a Postgres string literal with standard_conforming_strings on (the default since 9.1); the injection in searchNotifications is in the identifier position quote() never touches, and that is reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: TLS verification is disabled for the billing client
ruled_out.killed_by: The branch is guarded by `if Env == "sandbox"` where Env is `const Env = "production"` at main.go:24; the InsecureSkipVerify config is unreachable in this build.

ruled_out.assertion: echoEvent reflects the request body into HTML without escaping
ruled_out.killed_by: No route registers it: router.go declares only Health, Webhook.Billing, the device and sync handlers; grep for echoEvent returns the definition alone.

ruled_out.assertion: The billing webhook compares the signature against a digest that was already consumed
ruled_out.killed_by: hash.Sum(b) appends the current digest to b without mutating the hash state, so mac.Sum(nil) at line 63 equals want computed at line 60; the comparison is correct and uses hmac.Equal. The unused `want` variable is what makes it read as a defect.

ruled_out.assertion: ListDevices interpolates LIMIT %s and is injectable
ruled_out.killed_by: The only caller converts a bounds-checked int (1..500, handlers/device.go:40) with strconv.Itoa, so no attacker-controlled string reaches the format string.

ruled_out.assertion: chi RealIP lets a caller spoof the rate-limit key with X-Forwarded-For
ruled_out.killed_by: The IP branch is only reached when Scope.UserID is empty, and PerUserRateLimit is registered exclusively at router.go:42, inside the group whose first middleware is RequireSession; both token parsers reject an empty subject (token.go:58, token.go:80), so the spoofable branch is unreachable. The real gap on the unauthenticated credential routes is reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: proxy_ssl_verify off disables upstream certificate validation
ruled_out.killed_by: No proxy_pass in relay.conf uses https, and no location references the relay_thumbs upstream at all; the directive also restates nginx's own default, so it changes nothing in what ships.

ruled_out.assertion: The /static/ alias allows path traversal out of the static root
ruled_out.killed_by: The traversal shape requires a location without a trailing slash against an alias with one; here both `location /static/` and `alias /srv/relay/static/;` end in a slash, so the prefix is stripped correctly.

ruled_out.assertion: The landing route opens a template file named by a path parameter
ruled_out.killed_by: safe_slug (app/deps.py:72-75) rejects anything that does not match ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,63}$ before the join, which excludes dots and separators, and the handler returns 404 on ValueError.

ruled_out.assertion: The unsubscribe page reflects the token parameter into HTML
ruled_out.killed_by: The value is inserted into element text, not an attribute or script, and both < and > are replaced before insertion; no injection primitive remains in that context.

ruled_out.assertion: applyDefaults is a recursive merge vulnerable to prototype pollution
ruled_out.killed_by: It has no caller anywhere in the project: grep returns the definition, its own recursive call and the export. No request path reaches it, so no untrusted object is merged.

ruled_out.assertion: The partner webhook HMAC covers an empty body because ctx.request.rawBody is never set
ruled_out.killed_by: server.js:53 enables includeUnparsed on koa-bodyparser, which passes returnRawBody to co-body and assigns the raw string to ctx.request.rawBody; the digest at webhook.js:30 therefore covers the body.

ruled_out.assertion: callbackUrl reaches an outbound request from the worker (stored SSRF)
ruled_out.killed_by: No consumer exists in this tree: neither processor reads job.data.callbackUrl, and no HTTP client outside render.js appears in the project. The token's exposure through the failure log is reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: adminPolicyStatement grants Action * on Resource *
ruled_out.killed_by: The function is exported and never called: api-stack.ts imports ServiceRole, grantArtifacts and grantQueue only, and no other file references it. The privilege that is actually attached comes from attachTierPolicy and is reported as its own finding.

ruled_out.assertion: docs.exampleApiKey is a committed API key
ruled_out.killed_by: The object is documented at line 76 as onboarding sample values and no stack reads it; grep for exampleApiKey and exampleAccount returns only the declaration.

ruled_out.assertion: The job queue policy grants sqs:SendMessage to AnyPrincipal
ruled_out.killed_by: The statement carries an ArnEquals condition on aws:SourceArn (queue.ts:42-44) which pins the publisher, and the whole block is skipped because DataStack never passes eventBusArn (data-stack.ts:34-36).

findings.title: Admin API is registered outside the authenticated scope, so /admin/* needs no session
findings.evidence: server.js:27-34 registers authPlugin inside the encapsulated plugin `apiScope` mounted at /api/v1; Fastify hooks added with addHook inside a plugin apply only to that context and its children. server.js:38 registers adminRoutes on the root instance, a sibling context, so the onRequest session hook in plugins/auth.js:40 never runs for it. The decorator `requireRole` (plugins/auth.js:58) is defined inside the same encapsulated scope and is never called by any handler (grep over the tree returns only its definition). routes/admin.js:15 corroborates this: it falls back to 'system' because request.user is undefined outside apiScope.
findings.impact: Any unauthenticated caller can read every tenant's notifications (GET /admin/tenants/:id/notifications), delete a tenant and all of its notifications (DELETE /admin/tenants/:id -> lib/store.js:94), read the service configuration including trustedProxies, publicPrefixes and defaults (GET /admin/config), and query the session table by hash (POST /admin/sessions/impersonate).
findings.recommendation: Register adminRoutes inside a scope that first registers authPlugin, and call fastify.requireRole(request, 'operator') in every admin handler; add a test that asserts 401 for /admin/* with no Authorization header.

triage.reason: No unskippable layer covers it: the only auth is the onRequest hook in the /api/v1 scope, and Fastify encapsulation keeps it out of the root context where /admin is mounted.
The route file is imported and registered unconditionally in the shipped server.js:38; no flag guards it.
The second principal is any internet caller against an operator surface over tenant data.

findings.title: SQL injection through the filter map keys of POST /api/v1/notifications/search
findings.evidence: lib/store.js:51-53 builds predicates as `${column} = ${quote(value)}` from Object.entries(filter). Only the value passes quote() (store.js:19); the key is interpolated verbatim into the WHERE clause at store.js:58. The Fastify schema at routes/notifications.js:22-25 constrains additionalProperties to {type:'string'}, which restricts the values, not the property names, and declares no propertyNames constraint, so a body such as {"filter":{"1=1 OR tenant_id":"x"}} reaches the query builder intact.
findings.impact: An authenticated user of any tenant can alter the WHERE clause of a query issued by the application database role, reading rows outside the intended predicate and using boolean or subquery constructs to reach other tables.
findings.recommendation: Validate filter keys against an allowlist of real column names before building the predicate, or bind them through a mapping table; add propertyNames to the JSON schema.

triage.reason: The only control on the path is quote(), which is applied to the value and never to the key.
The keys come straight from the JSON request body of an authenticated route.
quote() is a correct literal-quoting helper, which is why it reads as safe; the injection is in the identifier position it does not cover.

findings.title: notifications/search runs with no tenant predicate, returning other tenants' rows
findings.evidence: routes/notifications.js:47-49 calls store.searchNotifications(request.body.filter) and never passes request.user.tenantId, unlike its siblings at lines 34 and 38 which both scope on request.user.tenantId. lib/store.js:54 uses 'TRUE' when the filter is empty and adds no tenant condition in any branch; the query at store.js:56 selects tenant_id, subject and recipient across the whole table with LIMIT 200.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user reads notification subjects and recipient addresses belonging to every other tenant, by posting an empty filter or one naming another tenant_id.
findings.recommendation: Add the caller's tenant to the predicate list server-side in searchNotifications and reject a client-supplied tenant_id key.

triage.reason: No middleware injects a tenant filter; the two sibling handlers pass it explicitly, which is the proof that nothing does it for them.
The rows carry recipient addresses, which are personal data under PRV-01.
Nothing marks this endpoint as a cross-tenant reporting surface; it is the dashboard's own filter panel.

findings.title: Template preview evaluates request-supplied expressions with new Function
findings.evidence: lib/render.js:25-30: for a `{{= ... }}` marker the body of the marker is compiled with `new Function(...keys, 'return (' + body + ');')` and executed. routes/notifications.js:58-61 exposes POST /api/v1/notifications/preview and passes the request body's `template` field into renderTemplate with no allowlist, no sandbox and no length or character restriction beyond the regex's exclusion of '}'. escapeHtml is applied to the result, after evaluation has already happened.
findings.impact: Any caller holding a session executes arbitrary JavaScript in the API process, which reaches process.env (DATABASE_URL, PULSE_WEBHOOK_SECRET) and the host through require('child_process').
findings.recommendation: Remove the `{{= }}` expression form, or evaluate it with a real expression interpreter restricted to property access over the variables object; never compile template text with new Function.

triage.reason: No sandbox, allowlist or parser sits between the request body and the Function constructor.
The sink is the Function constructor, which compiles and runs the string; escapeHtml only touches the return value.
The route is registered unconditionally inside the API scope in the shipped code.

findings.title: Webhook signature check runs only when the caller chooses to send a signature
findings.evidence: routes/webhooks.js:44 wraps the drift check and the HMAC comparison in `if (header)`, where header is request.headers[config.webhook.header] (x-pulse-signature). Omitting the header skips lines 45-53 entirely and execution continues to the write loop at line 57. The comment at 42-43 states the intent; the effect is that verification is optional for every caller, not only for the unmigrated providers.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller writes arbitrary rows into `deliveries` (lib/store.js:85), setting the delivery status of any provider_id, since the upsert keys on the attacker-supplied event.id.
findings.recommendation: Require the signature unconditionally; if legacy providers must be tolerated, gate them on a per-account flag looked up server-side rather than on the presence of a request header.

triage.reason: The signature check is the only control on this route; it is registered outside the /api/v1 auth scope by design (server.js:42).
The predicate that decides whether the control runs is a request header, i.e. fully attacker-controlled.
No flag guards this branch; it is the shipped code path.

findings.title: public-digest is matched by a public prefix and returns any tenant's recipients
findings.evidence: plugins/auth.js:13-16 skips the session hook for any URL whose path starts with an entry of config.publicPrefixes, which includes '/api/v1/notifications/public' (config/default.json:13). '/api/v1/notifications/public-digest/<tenantId>' satisfies that startsWith test, so the route at routes/notifications.js:53 runs with no session; it passes the path parameter straight to store.publicDigest (lib/store.js:73), which selects subject, recipient and status for that tenant with no other predicate and no token check.
findings.impact: Anyone who guesses or enumerates a tenant identifier reads the 25 most recent notification subjects and recipient addresses of that tenant without any credential.
findings.recommendation: Address the digest by an unguessable, expiring per-recipient token rather than by tenant id, and make the public prefix an exact path match instead of a startsWith over a family of routes.

triage.reason: The prefix rule at plugins/auth.js:15 disables the only control rather than compensating for it.

The intended exposure is one recipient's own digest reached from a mail client; the implementation exposes a whole tenant to any caller, so the finding moves to the missing capability token rather than disappearing.
recipient is an e-mail address or phone number, personal data under PRV-01.

findings.title: Error handler returns the raw exception message to the client
findings.evidence: server.js:46-49 sends `{ error: err.message }` with err.statusCode || 500 for every unhandled error in the application, including driver errors. The pg driver's messages carry the failing SQL fragment, column and relation names; store.js:55 issues a query built by string concatenation whose syntax errors therefore reach the caller.
findings.impact: Reconnaissance is cheap: internal identifiers, schema names and library errors leak to any caller, and the search endpoint's injection becomes error-based rather than blind.
findings.recommendation: Return a generic message plus a correlation id, and log the detail server-side only.

triage.reason: No filter or mapping sits between the exception and the response body.
It is not defence in depth: this is the sole error path for every route in the service.

findings.title: Rate-limit state is a per-process Map that is never evicted
findings.evidence: plugins/ratelimit.js:29 creates `const buckets = new Map()`; entries are added at line 41 keyed by request.user.id or request.ip and are only ever replaced, never deleted, until onClose (line 52). There is no size cap and no periodic sweep, and the counter is per process, so the configured max of 300/minute (config/default.json:16) multiplies by the number of workers.
findings.impact: A caller rotating source addresses grows the map without bound in the API process, and the same rotation dilutes the limit itself across processes.
findings.recommendation: Use a shared store with expiry (the Redis-backed limiter the comment declines) or add a TTL sweep and a maximum entry count.

triage.reason: No eviction, cap or external store exists in the plugin or its configuration.
There is no second implementation of the limit; this is the only one.

findings.title: The ops-token guard tests a prefix the maintenance blueprint is not mounted at
findings.evidence: auth.py:13 sets INTERNAL_PREFIX = '/internal' and auth.py:55 returns immediately unless request.path starts with it. app.py:35 registers internal_bp with url_prefix='/api/internal', so request.path for every maintenance endpoint is '/api/internal/...' and never matches; the abort(403) at auth.py:61 is unreachable. internal_bp also has no before_request(require_session), unlike api_bp (blueprints/api.py:16).
findings.impact: All four maintenance endpoints are reachable with no session and no ops header: GET /api/internal/status, POST /api/internal/import (arbitrary staged file into an arbitrary tenant), POST /api/internal/reindex, and DELETE /api/internal/tenants/<id>, which deletes every posting of a tenant (blueprints/internal.py:51).
findings.recommendation: Derive the guard from the blueprint rather than from a hard-coded string (register it as internal_bp.before_request), and add require_session to the blueprint; add a test asserting 403 without the header.

triage.reason: The compensating control is precisely the one that never runs; nothing else guards the blueprint.
Both the guard and the blueprint registration are in the shipped application factory.
The endpoints bind on the app's public listener and act across tenants.

findings.title: Hard-coded fallback SECRET_KEY signs the session cookie
findings.evidence: config.py:15 sets SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get('LEDGER_SECRET_KEY', 'ledger-flow-default-secret'), and the comment above it states this key signs the session cookie and the CSRF tokens. Nothing in the tree defines LEDGER_SECRET_KEY (no .env, no compose file, no deployment manifest in this repository), so the literal is the value in force wherever the variable is not injected. auth.py:24 trusts session['uid'] to resolve the user.
findings.impact: Anyone with this repository can mint a Flask session cookie carrying an arbitrary uid and be authenticated as that user, including an accountant-role user which passes require_role at auth.py:77.
findings.recommendation: Fail to start when LEDGER_SECRET_KEY is absent, and rotate the key; treat the literal as compromised.

triage.reason: INF-24 is explicit that a known placeholder is a finding because the value is identical in every deployment that forgot the variable, not because an attacker chose it.
No exported variable list or deployment manifest is present in this tree to show the variable is injected in production; absence of evidence cannot be HOLDS.
The default is in the production config class (ProductionConfig inherits BaseConfig at config.py:38).

findings.title: pickle.loads on a request form field
findings.evidence: blueprints/api.py:78-79 reads request.form['state'], base64-decodes it and passes it to pickle.loads with no integrity check, no allowlist and no type restriction. The blueprint requires only a resolved session (api.py:16).
findings.impact: Any authenticated user executes arbitrary code in the ledger process during unpickling, reaching the database credentials and the import volume.
findings.recommendation: Serialise drafts as JSON into a declared schema; if a binary form is required, sign it with a server key and verify before deserialising.

triage.reason: No HMAC or signature is verified before the loads call.
pickle reconstructs arbitrary objects and executes during reconstruction; this is the sink itself.
The blob is a request form field.

findings.title: Report views are unauthenticated and take the tenant from the query string
findings.evidence: reports_bp registers no before_request guard (contrast blueprints/api.py:16). auth.py:20-21 sets g.user = None for a request with no cookie and no bearer token, and current_tenant (auth.py:92-95) then returns request.args.get('tenant'). All three report views call it (reports.py:50, 72, 91) and pass the result straight into _rows_for, whose only predicate is that tenant (reports.py:41).
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller reads the full ledger of any tenant whose identifier it knows or guesses: /reports/statement?tenant=X, /reports/export.csv?tenant=X (up to 100000 postings) and /reports/trial-balance?tenant=X.
findings.recommendation: Add reports_bp.before_request(require_session) and drop the query-string fallback in current_tenant; if the nightly job needs it, give the job its own authenticated principal.

triage.reason: No middleware, decorator or ORM scope enforces the tenant; the fallback exists precisely to bypass it.
The docstring's intended exposure is a nightly export job, which is a credentialed caller, not an anonymous one.
Postings are financial records with free-text memos.

findings.title: The bulk import path skips Posting.clean(), and statements render memos as markup
findings.evidence: models.py:60-80 defines clean() as the invariant every posting must satisfy, including bleach.clean of the memo against ALLOWED_MEMO_TAGS. services/postings.py:17 calls it on the API write path. services/importer.py:67-82 builds plain dicts and calls db.session.bulk_insert_mappings, which writes rows without instantiating the model, so neither the account-code regex nor the memo sanitisation runs. blueprints/reports.py:64 then wraps the stored memo in Markup(), which is explicitly not escaped by Jinja when the template renders {{ row.memo }} at reports.py:30.
findings.impact: A memo containing script markup, arriving through the (unauthenticated, see the ops-token finding) import endpoint or from any bank file, executes in the browser of every user who opens that tenant's statement.
findings.recommendation: Route the importer through Posting.clean() (or apply bleach.clean to the mapping before insert) and stop marking stored memos as Markup; sanitise at render time instead.

triage.reason: The sanitiser exists but no code path applies it to imported rows; bulk_insert_mappings bypasses the ORM instance entirely.
memo comes from a CSV column of a staged file whose content and name are supplied to POST /api/internal/import.
No CSP is set anywhere in the application, so nothing bounds the impact.

findings.title: CSV export writes cell values with no formula neutralisation
findings.evidence: reports.py:80 writes entry_id, account_code, debit, credit and memo directly with csv.writer. memo and entry_id are attacker-influenced on the import path (services/importer.py:70-74 stores them verbatim), and no value is prefixed or quoted against leading '=', '+', '-' or '@'.
findings.impact: A memo beginning with '=' becomes a live formula when an accountant opens the export in a spreadsheet, which in Excel reaches DDE and external data fetches on the accountant's workstation.
findings.recommendation: Prefix any cell whose first character is '=', '+', '-', '@', tab or CR with an apostrophe, or export a format that has no formula semantics.

triage.reason: The values originate in imported CSV content and in API-supplied memos.
The declared mimetype is text/csv with an attachment disposition, which is the form spreadsheets open as a formula-bearing document.
The consumer is the accountants' workstation named in the module docstring.

findings.title: Maintenance status endpoint returns the database URI
findings.evidence: blueprints/internal.py:16-21 returns current_app.config['SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI'] and IMPORT_ROOT in the JSON response body. The URI is the value from config.py:17, a postgresql+psycopg DSN which carries the database password in deployments that use one. The endpoint is reachable with no credential (see the ops-token finding).
findings.impact: The database connection string, including its password, is disclosed in an HTTP response, together with the filesystem path the importer reads from.
findings.recommendation: Return a redacted health summary (driver, host, reachable yes/no) and never serialise configuration values into a response.

triage.reason: A connection string with credentials is exactly the data class this rule protects.
The guard that was meant to protect this endpoint never runs; see the ops-token finding.
There is no other control that keeps the value out of the response.

findings.title: Legacy token fallback accepts an unverified JWT payload
findings.evidence: internal/token/token.go:67-87 (ParseLegacy) splits the token on '.', base64url-decodes the middle segment and unmarshals it into Claims; it never computes or compares a signature and never checks the algorithm. middleware/auth.go:51-61 calls the real verifier first and, on any error including a bad signature, falls back to ParseLegacy; the resulting Claims populate Scope.UserID, TenantID and Role at auth.go:63-68.
findings.impact: Anyone can forge a token of the form <any>.<base64url payload>.<any> carrying sub, tid, role and a future exp and be authenticated as any user of any tenant with any role, on every route behind RequireSession and on RequireRole, which compares only Scope.Role.
findings.recommendation: Delete ParseLegacy and the fallback; if unmigrated handsets must be tolerated, verify them against the old key with a real signature check and a hard cut-off date.

triage.reason: The Verifier.Parse path is skipped by construction whenever it fails, so it is not a control on this path.
The decoded claims are used as the authenticated identity, not for logging or metrics.
The fallback is compiled unconditionally; no build tag or flag removes it.

findings.title: The /v1/sync routes are mounted outside the group that requires a session
findings.evidence: router.go:40-49 puts RequireSession and PerUserRateLimit on an inline chi Group covering /v1/profile, /v1/devices, /v1/devices/import and /v1/records. router.go:53-60 declares /v1/sync with r.Route, a separate subrouter whose only middlewares are Timeout and MaxBytes; a chi Group's middlewares apply to that group's routes only. The global stack (router.go:27-31) contains no authentication.
findings.impact: GET /v1/sync/delta, POST /v1/sync/push and GET /v1/sync/attachment are reachable with no credential at all, which turns the device-id and attachment-name defects below into unauthenticated read and write of other accounts' data.
findings.recommendation: Move the /v1/sync subrouter inside the authenticated group (or add pr.Use(RequireSession) to it) and assert 401 for each of the three paths in a router test.

triage.reason: No handler in handlers/sync.go re-checks the scope; Delta and Push accept a bare Scope{} without complaint.
The server binds :8080 for the mobile fleet (main.go:69); the caller is a second principal.
The comment explains the separate timeout and body cap, not an intended anonymous surface.

findings.title: Attachment handler joins an unvalidated name onto the attachment directory
findings.evidence: handlers/sync.go:128-138 reads the `name` query parameter, rejects only the empty string, and calls os.Open(filepath.Join(h.attachDir, name)). filepath.Join cleans the result but does not confine it: '../' segments resolve outside attachDir, and an absolute name makes the join absolute. attachDir is os.Getenv("ATLAS_ATTACHMENT_DIR") (main.go:63) with no default and no definition anywhere in this repository, so when the variable is unset the base is the empty string and every read is resolved against the process working directory.
findings.impact: Any caller (unauthenticated, per the routing finding) reads arbitrary files the service user can open and receives them as application/octet-stream.
findings.recommendation: Reject names that are not a bare generated identifier (regex on [A-Za-z0-9_-]), resolve with filepath.Clean and verify the result still has the base directory as a prefix, and fail closed when ATLAS_ATTACHMENT_DIR is unset.

triage.reason: There is no canonicalisation or prefix check between the parameter and os.Open.
The name comes from the query string; the comment calling it an opaque client-SDK identifier describes intent, not enforcement.
The sink is os.Open followed by io.Copy to the response body.

findings.title: ORDER BY column interpolated from the sort query parameter
findings.evidence: handlers/sync.go:113-117 reads r.URL.Query().Get("sort"), defaults it to 'updated_at' only when empty, and passes it to Repo.ListRecords. store/queries.go:162-169 builds the statement with fmt.Sprintf and places the value directly after ORDER BY; only ownerID is bound as $1.
findings.impact: An authenticated caller controls a SQL fragment in a query issued by the application role. lib/pq's extended protocol blocks stacked statements, but a subquery in the ORDER BY position yields boolean and error-based extraction of any table the role can read.
findings.recommendation: Map the sort parameter through a fixed allowlist of column names ('updated_at', 'kind', ...) and reject anything else.

triage.reason: No allowlist or column-name validation exists on the path; the default assignment only covers the empty string.
The value is a raw query-string parameter.
The sink is QueryContext on the assembled string; ORDER BY is an expression position, not a literal.

findings.title: Device identity is taken from the query string and record queries carry no owner predicate
findings.evidence: handlers/sync.go:39-44 returns the token's DeviceID when present and otherwise r.URL.Query().Get("device_id"). Delta (sync.go:48) and Push (sync.go:79) build on that value, and store/queries.go:145-152 (RecordsForDevice) filters on device_id alone with no owner or tenant condition. Push resolves the owner from the device itself (sync.go:95, queries.go:67), so the record is written into whichever account owns the named device.
findings.impact: Naming another handset's device_id reads that device's records and writes records into its owner's account. Combined with the /v1/sync routing finding, no credential is needed at all.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the device only from the authenticated scope, verify that the device belongs to the caller before any query, and add the owner column to the WHERE clause of RecordsForDevice.

triage.reason: No layer maps the device to the caller; the pairing table the comment mentions is never consulted in this tree.
device_id is a query-string parameter on the fallback branch.
The intended exposure is pre-3.2 handsets acting for their own account, which the code never verifies.

findings.title: Backup import writes records under an owner id taken from the request body
findings.evidence: handlers/device.go:81-95 decodes []store.Record from the body and passes it to BulkInsertRecords without reading middleware.ScopeFrom at all, so the caller's identity is never used. store/queries.go:121-142 inserts rec.OwnerID as given, and its ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE clause has no owner predicate, unlike UpsertRecord at queries.go:115 which carries `WHERE records.owner_id = $2`. The asymmetry between the two sibling writers is visible in the same file.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user creates records owned by any other user and, by reusing a known record id, overwrites the body of any existing record in the table regardless of owner.
findings.recommendation: Ignore OwnerID from the wire and set it from the authenticated scope; add the owner predicate to the upsert so a conflicting id belonging to someone else fails.

triage.reason: No scope check exists in the handler and none in the repository method; the guard present on the sibling writer proves it is not applied by a shared layer.
OwnerID is a JSON field of the request body (store/queries.go:42).
The docstring's 'restore lands where it belongs' is the intent that makes the field authoritative; it is not a bound.

findings.title: Token issuance binds a device id the caller supplies without verifying ownership
findings.evidence: handlers/device.go:104-131 authenticates the password with bcrypt and then mints a token whose DeviceID is creds.DeviceID, straight from the request body, with no lookup that the device belongs to user.ID (contrast CreateDevice at queries.go:75, which does bind the owner).
findings.impact: A user with valid credentials of their own obtains a token whose device claim names another account's handset, which the sync handlers then treat as the authorised device (see the device-identity finding), reading and writing that handset's records.
findings.recommendation: Look the device up by id and reject issuance when its user_id is not the authenticating user.

triage.reason: No verification of the device-to-user relation exists on this path.
DeviceID is a field of the credentials JSON body.
The boundary crossed is between two accounts of the same service.

findings.title: Credential endpoints carry no rate limiting
findings.evidence: PerUserRateLimit is applied only inside the authenticated group (router.go:42). /auth/token and /auth/refresh are registered at router.go:63-64 on the bare router, whose global middlewares (router.go:27-31) are RequestID, RealIP, Recoverer, SecurityHeaders and Timeout. There is no lockout, backoff or attempt counter in handlers/device.go:104-131, and no failed-login logging anywhere in the service.
findings.impact: Password guessing against /auth/token is unthrottled and unrecorded; bcrypt's cost is the only brake, and nothing detects the attempt.
findings.recommendation: Apply a limiter keyed on the submitted identity and on the source address to the credential routes, and log failures.

triage.reason: The limiter exists in the codebase but is not registered on these routes; a control that is not on the path is not a control.
The credential routes are intentionally unauthenticated, which is what makes the missing throttle the finding rather than the exposure; nothing bounds the attempt rate.
There is no server-side equivalent elsewhere: PerUserRateLimit is the only limiter in the module and it is registered on one group that does not include these routes.

findings.title: The import route has neither the body cap nor the batch cap its sibling enforces
findings.evidence: handlers/sync.go:90-93 rejects a batch above h.maxRecords (2000, set at sync.go:23) and its route sits behind MaxBytes(8<<20) (router.go:55). The sibling importer at handlers/device.go:81 decodes []store.Record from an uncapped body — /v1/devices/import is in the group at router.go:47, which has no MaxBytes — and checks only for the empty case at line 87 before inserting every element in a single transaction.
findings.impact: One authenticated request with a large JSON array is decoded into memory and inserted row by row inside one transaction, exhausting memory and holding database locks.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the group with MaxBytes and apply the same maxRecords ceiling in Import.

triage.reason: No body limit is configured on the server (main.go:68-74 sets only timeouts) nor on this group.
The array length and every element's size come from the request body, so the allocation is sized by the peer.
The route is reachable by any authenticated user of the fleet, and the sibling that enforces both caps is the proof that the bound is meant to exist.

findings.title: The edge ACL guards /internal/ while the operator API is mounted at /ops
findings.evidence: nginx/relay.conf:25-31 restricts /internal/ to two office ranges and denies everything else. The application serves no path under /internal: app/main.py:28 mounts the operator routes at /ops. Requests to /ops/* therefore fall through to `location /` (relay.conf:56) and are proxied with no address restriction, no rate limit and no connection cap. routes_admin.py:3-5 states in its docstring that the handlers do not re-check membership because the edge only forwards them from the office ranges.
findings.impact: The whole operator surface — feature flags, webhook replay and tenant purge — is reachable from any network location, with the application relying on a network control that applies to a path it does not serve.
findings.recommendation: Point the location block at the prefix the application actually serves (/ops/), and stop treating a proxy ACL as the only authorisation for state-changing operator endpoints.

triage.reason: The control exists but sits on a path with no routes behind it; the routes that need it are matched by `location /`.
The intended exposure is staff-only; the finding is that nothing enforces it.
There is no rewrite, alias or upstream mapping in relay.conf or upstreams.conf that would turn /ops into /internal.

findings.title: /ops/status is declared public and returns RELAY_DATABASE_URL
findings.evidence: app/deps.py:11-15 lists '/ops/status' among the paths that answer before a session exists, and app/middleware.py:43-45 returns early for them with request.state.user = None. app/routes_admin.py:21-32 returns settings.database_url, which is os.environ['RELAY_DATABASE_URL'] (deps.py:27), together with the operator audience, the template directory and the pid. docker-compose.yml:21 shows that URL is postgresql://relay:<password>@db:5432/relay.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller reads the database connection string with its password, plus internal paths and the process id used for further reconnaissance.
findings.recommendation: Remove /ops/status from PUBLIC_PATHS, and return only a boolean liveness result rather than configuration values.

triage.reason: A DSN carrying a password is exactly the data class this rule protects.
The public-path list disables the session middleware for this route; no other control applies (see the /ops ACL finding).
The intended exposure is a liveness widget, which needs none of these fields; the finding moves to the payload.

findings.title: Operator handlers perform no role check, so any session can purge a tenant
findings.evidence: app/routes_admin.py:35-60 contains no reference to request.state.user or to any role: flags() mutates the module-level _FLAGS dict on POST (line 42), replay() acts on a delivery id from the body, and purge_tenant() acts on a path parameter. app/middleware.py:64 attaches whatever claims the cookie carried without inspecting a role, and there is no dependency, decorator or second middleware between the router and these handlers.
findings.impact: Any holder of a valid relay_session cookie — that is, any tenant user of the platform — flips feature flags for everyone, replays webhook deliveries against arbitrary tenants and issues tenant purges.
findings.recommendation: Require an operator role claim in each handler (or in a Mount-level middleware over /ops) and fail closed when the claim is absent.

triage.reason: SessionAuthMiddleware authenticates but never authorises; nothing else runs before these handlers.
The docstring's assumption of a staff-only network is not enforced anywhere reachable (see the /ops ACL finding).
The second principal is any ordinary tenant user of the same deployment.

findings.title: The edge reflects the request Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
findings.evidence: nginx/relay.conf:39-41 emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin $http_origin` unconditionally together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials true` for everything under /api/, which includes the authenticated /api/whoami (app/routes_public.py:75) and /api/preview. There is no origin allowlist, no map block and no exact comparison anywhere in the two nginx files.
findings.impact: Any web page a logged-in user visits can read authenticated API responses with the relay_session cookie attached, because the browser is told every origin is allowed and that credentials may be sent.
findings.recommendation: Replace the reflection with a map of exact allowed origins (the per-tenant subdomains) and emit the header only for a match.

triage.reason: No allowlist exists at the edge or in the application; the value is copied from the request header.
/api/whoami returns the session claims and the caller's address.
`$http_origin` is the request's Origin header verbatim, not a validated variable.

findings.title: Link preview fetches any URL the caller supplies
findings.evidence: app/routes_public.py:28-46 takes the `url` query parameter, rejects only the empty value, and issues httpx.AsyncClient(...).get(target) with follow_redirects=True. No scheme check, no host allowlist, no address-family or private-range check and no egress proxy appears anywhere in the module or in deps.py. The response's status code, content-type and <title> are returned to the caller.
findings.impact: The service performs requests from inside the compose network and the cloud VPC: http://thumbs:8100, http://db:5432, http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ and other internal endpoints, with the status, content type and title reflected back, and redirects followed to reach targets that a naive allowlist would have blocked.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the host, reject non-public addresses and non-http(s) schemes before connecting, disable redirect following (or re-validate every hop), and route the fetch through an egress proxy with an allowlist.

triage.reason: No validation runs between the query parameter and the client call.
target is a request query parameter.
The intended exposure is fetching a tenant-pasted public link; nothing bounds it to public addresses.

findings.title: The application container publishes port 8000 on the host, bypassing the edge
findings.evidence: docker-compose.yml:24-27 maps 8000:8000 for the app service with the comment that the load tester and the on-call debugger reach the service without going through the edge. Everything the edge provides — the /internal/ address ACL (relay.conf:25), limit_req and limit_conn on /api/ (relay.conf:34-35), the security headers (relay.conf:19-21) and the body-size cap (relay.conf:10) — is absent on that port.
findings.impact: Anyone able to reach the host on 8000 gets the unprotected application: no rate limiting, no body cap, no security headers and no address restriction.
findings.recommendation: Use `expose` instead of `ports` so the service is reachable only on the compose network, and give the load tester and debugger a route through the edge or an SSH tunnel.

triage.reason: The exposure is intended for two internal consumers but is bounded by nothing: the mapping listens on all host interfaces.
The application implements none of the edge's controls itself.
The published port crosses from the container network to the host network.

findings.title: An x-debug-user header grants the operator role whenever RELAY_ENV is unset
findings.evidence: app/middleware.py:47-53 accepts the x-debug-user header as a full identity with role 'operator' when settings.is_local. deps.py:41-42 defines is_local as env == 'local', and deps.py:26 defaults RELAY_ENV to 'local' when the variable is absent. The only definition of RELAY_ENV in the tree is docker-compose.yml:20; any other way of starting `uvicorn app.main:app` (including the debugger path the compose file itself advertises on port 8000) leaves the default in force.
findings.impact: In any deployment that does not set RELAY_ENV, a single request header makes the caller an operator, which combined with the /ops handlers' lack of a role check means flag changes and tenant purges.
findings.recommendation: Make the debug identity opt in through an explicit RELAY_ALLOW_DEBUG_USER flag that defaults to off, and make the environment default to the most restricted value rather than 'local'.

triage.reason: docker-compose.yml sets RELAY_ENV=production for the container, but that is one deployment descriptor and the tree contains no other; whether every shipped deployment sets it cannot be established here, so this caps the finding at probable.
The identity is read from a request header the caller chooses.
No layer re-checks the role granted on this branch.

findings.title: Session cookie claims are never checked for expiry
findings.evidence: app/middleware.py:17-34 verifies the HMAC and returns the decoded JSON claims; neither _unsign nor dispatch (lines 59-64) reads an exp, iat or nbf field, and no other module in the tree inspects the claims. There is no revocation lookup and no absolute lifetime.
findings.impact: A cookie captured once stays valid for as long as the signing key does; a sign-out cannot invalidate it server-side.
findings.recommendation: Include and verify an expiry in the signed payload, keep an absolute lifetime, and check a server-side revocation list for operator sessions.

triage.reason: The sign-in service that mints the cookie is outside this repository, so whether the payload even carries an expiry cannot be established here; that keeps this at probable.
No layer in this tree enforces a session lifetime; the cookie's own Max-Age would bind only a cooperative browser.
There is no second control that limits session lifetime.

findings.title: Database password committed in docker-compose, and the app's DSN interpolates a variable nothing defines
findings.evidence: docker-compose.yml:43 sets POSTGRES_PASSWORD: relay_local_dev_only as a literal for the database service, while docker-compose.yml:21 builds the application's DSN from ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}, a shell variable that no file in this tree defines (no .env, no .env.example). The two therefore disagree unless an operator exports the variable, and the literal is readable by anyone with the repository.
findings.impact: The database credential is in version control, and the deployment silently starts with an empty password in the application DSN when the variable is not exported.
findings.recommendation: Move the password to a secret file or manager referenced by both services, keep it out of the repository, and rotate the committed value.

triage.reason: Per INF-24 a known placeholder is a finding because it is identical in every deployment that forgot the variable, and here it is also the value the database is actually created with.
docker-compose.yml is the shipped deployment descriptor of this service.
No outside control applies to the db service: the literal is inline in the shipped compose file and is the value the database is created with, so nothing external overrides it or un-commits it.

findings.title: The request path is written into a line-oriented log with no neutralisation
findings.evidence: Enumerated with tools/log_escaper.py: 2 logging calls in the Python sources, both UNCLEARED — middleware.py:61 (`log.info("rejected session cookie for %s", path)`) and middleware.py:71 (method, url.path, status). Both values come from the request line, and uvicorn percent-decodes the path into scope['path'], so %0d%0a in the URL becomes a real CRLF in the record. AccessLogMiddleware is listed first in main.py:32-35, so it wraps the auth middleware and logs unauthenticated requests too. No escaping or repr() is applied at either site.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller forges whole log records — a fabricated 'session accepted' line, or a line attributed to another user — which corrupts the record an incident would be reconstructed from and can inject markup into any viewer that renders the log as HTML.
findings.recommendation: Escape or JSON-encode the path and method before logging (or emit structured JSON records), and reject control characters in the path at the edge.

triage.reason: The path and method are taken verbatim from the request line and reach the sink undecorated.

The application attaches no handler or formatter (main.py:16 only sets a level), so the record format in production is decided by the deployment's logging configuration; a line-oriented handler makes this exploitable and a structured one does not, and that cannot be settled from this tree. This caps the finding at probable.
No other control preserves log integrity.

findings.title: Client address for the office check is taken from the first X-Forwarded-For entry
findings.evidence: app/deps.py:48-60 returns the first comma-separated element of X-Forwarded-For, falling back to X-Real-IP and only then to the socket peer. nginx sets X-Forwarded-For with $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for (relay.conf:16), which appends the peer to whatever the client sent, so the first element is always the caller's own value. from_office (deps.py:63-65) then prefix-matches that value against the office ranges, and routes_admin.py:53 returns the result.
findings.impact: Any caller can make client_ip and from_office report an office address by sending one header. Today the only consumer echoes it in a response body, so nothing is bypassed yet; the helper is nevertheless the wrong primitive for the staff decision its name and callers imply.
findings.recommendation: Take the peer address from the connection, or take the last untrusted-hop entry of X-Forwarded-For after validating the number of trusted proxies; never use the first element as an identity.

triage.reason: The value originates in a request header the caller sets.
The nginx allow/deny block uses $remote_addr and is not spoofable, but it guards /internal/, a path the application does not serve, so it is not a control on any path that reaches from_office.

findings.title: Job retry merges an arbitrary request body over the stored job payload
findings.evidence: src/api/routes.js:55-59 spreads `overrides = ctx.request.body` over previous.data and re-enqueues it. The ownership check on line 51 covers the job being retried, not the payload that replaces it, and schema.validateRenderJob is never called on this path, so none of the constraints of src/lib/schema.js:18-29 apply: tenantId (set from the session on submission, routes.js:22), documentId (^[a-f0-9]{24}$), template, width and assetBaseUrl (the ASSET_HOSTS allowlist at schema.js:74-81) are all overridable.
findings.impact: An authenticated user re-enqueues a job with another tenant's tenantId, with an assetBaseUrl pointing anywhere (see the render SSRF finding), and with a documentId containing path separators, which decides both the temporary file path written in the worker (processors/render.js:54) and the S3 key the artifact is stored under (render.js:64).
findings.recommendation: Whitelist the fields a retry may override (at most width and template) and re-run validateRenderJob on the merged payload; never let a retry set tenantId.

triage.reason: The validator exists but is not invoked on this route; the tenant check on line 51 validates a different object than the one enqueued.
overrides is the parsed JSON request body.
tenantId is the tenant boundary of the whole service.

findings.title: Partner webhook enqueues an export job that bypasses the filename and tenant validation
findings.evidence: src/api/webhook.js:46-53 calls queue.enqueueExport directly with tenantId: body.tenant_id and filename: body.filename. The sibling producer at src/api/routes.js:66-70 routes the same job through schema.validateExportJob, which applies the tenantId pattern ^[a-z0-9-]{3,40}$ and checkFilename's ^(\w+\.)*\w+$ (schema.js:16,35,87). The consumer trusts that: src/worker/processors/export.js:29-30 says payloads reach it already validated, and line 40 builds path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, tenantId, `${filename}.${format}`) with fs.mkdir(recursive) and fs.writeFile.
findings.impact: A caller holding a partner secret writes a file to an arbitrary path on the worker filesystem (filename '../../../../etc/cron.d/x'), and steers loadRows (export.js:17) at an arbitrary .tsv path through the same traversal in tenantId.
findings.recommendation: Call schema.validateExportJob on the webhook path as well, and re-validate tenantId and filename inside the processor before building the path.

triage.reason: The validator is on the sibling producer only; the processor explicitly declines to re-check.
Both values are fields of the webhook JSON body.
The signature bounds who may call, not what the payload may contain; a partner is still a second principal.

findings.title: The render worker fetches whatever assetBaseUrl the job carries
findings.evidence: processors/render.js:50-51 takes job.data.assetBaseUrl (defaulting to the constant) and calls fetchAssetManifest, which issues fetch(`${baseUrl}/manifest.json`) at render.js:21. The only host allowlist in the project is in the API's validator (src/lib/schema.js:74-81); the worker re-checks nothing, and the retry route (src/api/routes.js:57) enqueues jobs that never passed that validator.
findings.impact: The worker, which runs in the same network as Redis and S3, issues requests to any host and path an authenticated user chooses, including the cloud metadata endpoint; the fetched manifest.css value is then interpolated into the HTML the headless browser loads (render.js:57).
findings.recommendation: Re-validate assetBaseUrl against ASSET_HOSTS inside the processor before fetching, and disallow non-https schemes and redirects.

triage.reason: The allowlist is not on this path; the producer that applies it is not the only producer.
assetBaseUrl arrives in the job payload from a request body.
The intended egress is the three asset hosts, which nothing enforces here.

findings.title: Rendered tenant documents are uploaded public-read with a permanent URL
findings.evidence: processors/render.js:68-71 calls storage.putObject with { public: true }, which sets ACL 'public-read' and CacheControl public, max-age=31536000 (src/lib/storage.js:39-40), and returns storage.publicUrl(key) (storage.js:47), an address with no signature and no expiry. The comment on lines 66-67 states the address must not expire. The same module has a signedUrl path (storage.js:59) that the artifacts route uses, so the unsigned one is a deliberate second class of link.
findings.impact: Every rendered invoice, statement and letter is readable by anyone who obtains or guesses the object URL, permanently and with no revocation; the key is predictable once the tenant id and document id are known, and the retry route lets a caller choose both.
findings.recommendation: Store renders privately and hand out short-lived signed URLs, including in the e-mail; if a stable link is required, proxy it through an authenticated redirect.

triage.reason: The intended exposure is one customer reading their own document; a public-read ACL over a predictable key is not bounded to that.
The objects are customer invoices and statements.
No bucket policy, CDN signature or referrer check appears in this project to compensate.

findings.title: The worker logs the whole job payload on failure, including the callback token
findings.evidence: src/worker/index.js:30-41 logs `payload: job.data` for every failed job, with the comment at 28-29 explaining the intent. job.data carries callbackToken and callbackUrl, which src/api/routes.js:25-26 copies from the raw request body (bypassing the validated `data`, since renderJobSchema declares additionalProperties: false), plus the tenant identifiers and document ids of the failing job.
findings.impact: Third-party callback credentials and tenant payloads land in the log stream in clear text, so anyone with log access holds those tokens.
findings.recommendation: Redact known secret fields before logging (pino redact paths), or log a job id and fetch the payload from the queue when reproducing.

triage.reason: No redaction option is configured on the pino instance at index.js:10.
callbackToken is a bearer credential for the caller's own endpoint.
There is no other place the payload is protected; this is the only failure handler.

findings.title: Redis connection falls back to a hard-coded password
findings.evidence: src/queue/index.js:5-10 builds the BullMQ connection with host 127.0.0.1, port 6379 and password: process.env.REDIS_PASSWORD || 'orchard-local-dev'. No file in this project defines REDIS_PASSWORD (package.json's start scripts set only NODE_ENV), so the literal is the value in force wherever the variable is not injected, and it is shared by the API and the worker (src/worker/index.js:14,20).
findings.impact: A deployment that forgets the variable authenticates to Redis with a password published in this repository; whoever reaches the queue reads and writes job payloads, which are the service's whole work stream.
findings.recommendation: Fail to start when REDIS_PASSWORD is absent, and rotate the literal.

triage.reason: INF-24: the finding is that the default is known and identical in every deployment that forgot the variable, not that an attacker sets it.
No deployment manifest or variable list in this tree shows REDIS_PASSWORD being injected; without that artifact this is not HOLDS.
The fallback is in the module both production entry points import.

findings.title: Session tokens are signed but never expire
findings.evidence: src/api/server.js:13-33 verifies an HMAC over the payload and returns JSON.parse of it as ctx.state.user, with no reading of exp, iat or any lifetime, and no lookup against a store. The gate at server.js:62-74 accepts whatever that returns.
findings.impact: A token that leaks once authorises the service forever; there is no way to revoke it short of rotating ORCHARD_SESSION_SECRET for every user.
findings.recommendation: Include an expiry in the signed payload and reject stale tokens; keep a revocation list keyed on a token id.

triage.reason: No middleware or store check bounds the token's lifetime anywhere in the project.
There is no second control that limits validity.

decodeSession is the shipped gate: server.js:62-74 is the only authentication middleware in the application, and a bearer token has no browser-enforced lifetime to fall back on the way a cookie's Max-Age would.

findings.title: Artifact URLs are signed with SHA-256 over concatenated secret, key and expiry
findings.evidence: src/lib/storage.js:51-56 computes sha256(`${secret}${key}${expiresAt}`) — a raw hash with the secret as a prefix rather than an HMAC, and with no delimiter between the fields. verifySignedUrl (storage.js:65-71) recomputes it the same way and, at line 66, compares Number(expiresAt) which is NaN for a non-numeric value, so the expiry test passes for such input.
findings.impact: The construction is length-extendable and field-ambiguous (key 'a' with expiry '12' hashes identically to key 'a1' with expiry '2'), so signature validity does not pin the pair it was issued for. No verifier is present in this tree, so the exploitable consequence cannot be demonstrated here.
findings.recommendation: Use crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret) over a delimited canonical string, and reject a non-numeric expiry explicitly.

triage.reason: The digest governs access to a private artifact; it is a security decision, not a checksum.
verifySignedUrl has no caller in this tree (the CDN or edge that consumes these links is not present), so the impact of the ambiguity cannot be measured here; this caps the finding at probable.
No second signature or authorisation check accompanies the link in this codebase.

findings.title: Artifact keys are built by concatenating the tenant prefix with an unnormalised path parameter
findings.evidence: src/api/routes.js:75-81 signs `${ctx.state.user.tenantId}/${ctx.params.key}` with no canonicalisation and no rejection of dot segments. @koa/router matches :key against a non-slash pattern but decodes the capture afterwards, so a request path containing %2F and %2E yields a key such as '../../other-tenant/renders/x.pdf', and the signature is minted over that string.
findings.impact: A caller obtains a validly signed URL whose path escapes their own tenant prefix; whether it resolves to the other tenant's object depends on whether the serving layer normalises dot segments, which most HTTP caches and CDNs do.
findings.recommendation: Reject any key that is not a bare object name (allowlist [A-Za-z0-9._-]), and canonicalise before signing.

triage.reason: key is a path parameter of the request.
The component that serves PUBLIC_BASE and validates the signature is outside this tree, so whether it normalises the path cannot be established; this caps the finding at probable.
No canonicalisation or prefix re-check exists between the parameter and the signing call.

findings.title: The headless renderer runs with the sandbox disabled
findings.evidence: processors/render.js:32-41 invokes chromium-headless with --no-sandbox. The page it loads embeds a stylesheet URL taken from a remote manifest (render.js:57) whose origin the retry route lets a caller choose.
findings.impact: A browser-engine compromise while rendering attacker-influenced content escapes directly to the worker process, which holds the S3 credentials and the queue connection.
findings.recommendation: Keep the Chromium sandbox enabled (grant the container SYS_ADMIN-free user namespaces or run the browser as a non-root user with the sandbox intact).

triage.reason: No seccomp, user-namespace or container-level substitute is declared anywhere in this project.
The flag is a workaround for running as root in a container, not a bounded exposure.
No compensating isolation layer is present in the repository.

findings.title: The production API task role is given AdministratorAccess
findings.evidence: config/environments.ts:26-30 maps the 'ops' tier to the AWS managed policy 'AdministratorAccess', and prod sets apiTier: 'ops' (environments.ts:68). lib/constructs/service-role.ts:43-46 attaches that managed policy to the ECS task role, which lib/api-stack.ts:47 assigns as the taskRole of the Fargate task running beacon/api:1.12.0. The scoped grants the same stack adds (grantArtifacts, grantQueue, secret.grantRead at api-stack.ts:39-41) become irrelevant beside it.
findings.impact: Any code execution or SSRF in the production API container yields full administrative control of the AWS account through the task's credential endpoint.
findings.recommendation: Give the API the same 'standard' tier as the other environments and attach explicit statements for the maintenance actions the runbooks need; never attach AdministratorAccess to a task role.

triage.reason: No permissions boundary, SCP or condition appears anywhere in this project to trim the effective scope.
The comment at environments.ts:66-68 states the intent; nothing bounds it, and the maintenance commands are not enumerated.

This is not an absent defence in depth: the managed policy is the effective permission set of the running task, and the scoped grants beside it add nothing it does not already have. INF-01 invokes FP-01 and FP-05, both answered above.

findings.title: The artifact bucket is made world-readable for every object although it also holds tenant exports
findings.evidence: lib/constructs/bucket.ts:33-39 replaces BLOCK_ALL with a BlockPublicAccess that sets blockPublicPolicy: false and restrictPublicBuckets: false when publicRead is on, and lines 55-64 add a bucket policy granting s3:GetObject to iam.AnyPrincipal() over arnForObjects('*') — the whole bucket, not a brand-asset prefix. lib/data-stack.ts:26-32 passes publicRead: cfg.assetsPublic and its comment states that this single bucket holds the brand assets, the rendered documents and the tenant data exports; environments.ts:64 sets assetsPublic: true for prod.
findings.impact: Every rendered document and every tenant data export in production is readable anonymously by object key, with no CloudFront origin identity in between.
findings.recommendation: Scope the policy to the public prefix (arnForObjects('public/*')) and keep BLOCK_ALL otherwise, or split the public assets into their own bucket and serve it through a CDN with an origin access identity.

triage.reason: The intended exposure is the CDN reading brand assets; the statement covers every object, so the finding moves to the scope of the grant.
The same bucket holds tenant exports and rendered documents, per the comment in the stack that instantiates it.
enforceSSL and encryption do not limit who may read; no other condition narrows the principal.

findings.title: The dev bastion accepts SSH from the whole internet
findings.evidence: config/environments.ts:36 sets adminCidrs: ['0.0.0.0/0'] for dev, and lib/network-stack.ts:52-58 turns each entry into an ingress rule on tcp/22 of the bastion security group. The staging and prod entries are real ranges (environments.ts:49,62), so this is not the shape of every environment. The same bastion group is granted 5432 to the database (network-stack.ts:81-85).
findings.impact: Port 22 of the dev jump host is exposed to the internet for password or key-guessing, and that host is the one with a network path to the dev database.
findings.recommendation: Give dev a real operator range, and make the construct reject 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 outright.

triage.reason: This is not the public load balancer on 80/443; it is management access on 22, which the procedure classifies as a finding without further argument.
No NACL, managed firewall or session-manager-only policy is declared in this repository.
The dev account holds a real RDS instance created by the same stack set.

findings.title: An unset or unknown BEACON_ENV silently selects the dev configuration
findings.evidence: config/environments.ts:82-84 returns environments[name ?? ''] ?? dev, so both an absent variable and a typo ('production' instead of 'prod') resolve to dev. bin/beacon.ts:14 calls it with process.env.BEACON_ENV ?? app.node.tryGetContext('env') and derives the account, the region, the admin CIDRs, assetsPublic and ephemeral from the result.
findings.impact: A mistyped or missing stage variable deploys the permissive profile — SSH open to 0.0.0.0/0, a public bucket, RemovalPolicy.DESTROY with autoDeleteObjects and one NAT gateway — under whatever account credentials the pipeline holds.
findings.recommendation: Throw on an unknown or missing name instead of defaulting, and let the pipeline fail loudly.

triage.reason: INF-24: the default decides the security profile of the deployment and is identical wherever the variable is forgotten.
This is the shipped entry point used by cdk.json's app command.
No pipeline definition is present in this tree to show BEACON_ENV is always exported per stage.

findings.title: The API container is configured with a CORS wildcard and credentials enabled
findings.evidence: lib/api-stack.ts:53-61 sets CORS_ALLOW_ORIGIN: '*' together with CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS: 'true' in the container environment, with a comment explaining that the origin cannot be pinned. The combination is rejected by browsers when emitted literally, which is why implementations that honour both reflect the request Origin instead — the exact pattern the sibling service's edge already uses (edge-relay/nginx/relay.conf:39).
findings.impact: If the image honours the pair by reflecting the caller's Origin, any web page can read authenticated API responses with the user's credentials attached.
findings.recommendation: Pass an explicit list of allowed origins (the tenant subdomain suffix, matched exactly) and never combine a wildcard with credentials.

triage.reason: The consuming image beacon/api:1.12.0 is not in this tree, so how it interprets the pair cannot be established; the misconfiguration in the declaration is established, the runtime behaviour is not.
The values are literals in the stack, so the exposure is a deployment decision rather than an attacker input — which is what makes it a configuration finding.
No other declared setting bounds the origin.

findings.title: The RDS instance is declared publicly accessible
findings.evidence: lib/data-stack.ts:60 sets publiclyAccessible: true, with a comment that an analytics account pulls nightly over the public endpoint. The same resource is placed in PRIVATE_ISOLATED subnets (data-stack.ts:48) and its security group allows only the service and bastion groups (network-stack.ts:76-85), so the two declarations contradict each other.
findings.impact: The instance is given a public DNS name and the intent of internet reachability; today the isolated subnet and the security group keep it unreachable, so the finding is one broken layer of defence in depth plus a stated requirement that would be met by removing the remaining ones.
findings.recommendation: Set publiclyAccessible: false and give the analytics account a VPC peering, PrivateLink or replica path instead.

triage.reason: The isolated subnet and the security group do bound it today, but a subnet route change or one extra ingress rule removes that bound; this is a defence-in-depth layer that has been switched off rather than a compensated one.

The nightly analytics pull is a stated intended exposure, but no artifact in this tree shows how that account connects, so whether the flag is load-bearing cannot be established; this caps the finding at probable.
The property is set for every environment, production included.

findings.title: The artifact bucket construct promises access logs it never configures
findings.evidence: The construct's docstring (lib/constructs/bucket.ts:16-19) states the platform defaults are SSE, TLS-only access, versioning and access logs. The Bucket props at lines 29-53 set encryption, enforceSSL, versioned, blockPublicAccess, removalPolicy, autoDeleteObjects and lifecycleRules — there is no serverAccessLogsBucket or serverAccessLogsPrefix, and no CloudTrail data-event configuration appears anywhere in the stack set.
findings.impact: There is no record of who read the objects in the bucket that also serves them anonymously, so an exposure of tenant exports cannot be scoped or reconstructed.
findings.recommendation: Add serverAccessLogsBucket (or a CloudTrail data event selector) for this bucket, and keep the docstring and the props in step.

triage.reason: Logging could be centralised by an organisation-level policy outside this repository; per FP-08, without the exported artifact that is UNKNOWN and not HOLDS.
No other record of object access exists in the definition.
The bucket is not a scratch space: it holds tenant exports and public assets.
